procedural_history.originating_court: The case originated with an inquiry ordered by the Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh, which led to an investigation by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI).
procedural_history.impugned_order: The appellant challenged the order dated 5th July, 1968, placing him under suspension, made by the Government of India, Ministry of Home Affairs on 11 July, 1968.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court at Delhi challenging the suspension order. The High Court ruled against the appellant.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, having failed in the Delhi High Court, appealed to the Supreme Court by certificate. The Supreme Court was approached because the appellant contended that the suspension order was passed on a report made mala fide and that the order did not satisfy the conditions of Rule 7 of the All-India Service (Appeal and Discipline) Rules, 1955.

decision.appeal_result: The appeal, therefore, fails and is dismissed.
directions: each party should bear its costs in this Court

issue.issue_text: Whether the order of suspension was in violation of Rule 7 of the All-India Service (Appeal and Discipline) Rules, 1955, as the appellant contended it did not meet the criteria of sub-rule (1) and was not made under sub-rule (3).

facts: The appellant, a police officer, was placed under suspension by the Government of India.
The suspension followed an enquiry by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) into serious allegations of corruption and malpractices against him.

A First Information Report (FIR) had been filed against the appellant for offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act, and an investigation and trial relating to this criminal charge were pending.

The appellant argued that the suspension order was invalid because it was improperly made under sub-rule (1) of Rule 7, as no disciplinary proceedings had been initiated, and that it was not an order under sub-rule (3).
law: Rule 7 of the All-India Service (Appeal and Discipline) Rules, 1955, governs the suspension of service members.
Sub-rule (1) allows for suspension when a disciplinary proceeding is initiated against a member.
Sub-rule (3) allows the government, at its discretion, to suspend a member against whom an investigation, inquiry, or trial relating to a criminal charge is pending.
application: The Court first rejected the appellant's premise that the order was made under sub-rule (1). It observed that the suspension order itself made no reference to sub-rule (1).
Instead, the Court determined that the order was made under sub-rule (3).

The Court reasoned that the factual conditions for invoking sub-rule (3) were clearly met, as there was an ongoing investigation and a pending trial related to a criminal charge against the appellant.
It held that the suspension order must be read in the context of the entire case and the surrounding circumstances, which pointed to the pending criminal matter.

The Court also found that the appellant had failed to establish his claim of 'mala fides' (bad faith), as he made no specific allegations against any particular officer of the Government of India who issued the order.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's challenge, concluding that the suspension order was not in violation of Rule 7. The Court held that the order was not made under sub-rule (1), but was a valid exercise of power under sub-rule (3), given that an investigation and trial relating to a criminal charge were pending against the appellant.

issue.issue_text: Whether the suspension order was invalid because the report of the Central Bureau of Investigation was allegedly made mala fide.

facts: The appellant argued that his suspension order was invalid because the underlying report from the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) was made in bad faith (mala fide).
The appellant claimed this bad faith stemmed from the hostility of the Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh and the investigators themselves.
law: The Court's role is not to determine the correctness or propriety of an investigation report in this context.
The Court's inquiry is limited to examining whether the suspension order was (1) warranted by the relevant rule and (2) an honest exercise of the government's powers.
application: The Court separated the CBI's report from the government's suspension order.
It stated that the allegation of mala fides against the CBI was not the issue before it; the issue was the validity of the suspension order.
The Court noted that the appellant had not alleged that any specific officer of the Government of India (the authority that issued the suspension) had acted in bad faith.
The Court found that the suspension order itself satisfied the legal requirements and was an honest exercise of power by the government, which had considered the available material.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, concluding that the alleged mala fides of the Central Bureau of Investigation in preparing its report were not relevant. The Court's focus was on the suspension order itself, which it found to be a legally valid and honest exercise of power by the Government of India.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946, was ultra vires and the investigation was invalid.

facts: The appellant raised a legal challenge, arguing that the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946, was 'ultra vires' (beyond the legal power or authority) and that the investigation based on it was therefore invalid.
application: The appellant specifically requested that the Supreme Court not make a decision on this point in the current appeal.
The reason for this request was that the appellant intended to raise the same argument in a separate, pending criminal case that resulted from the investigation.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court did not decide the issue. It explicitly 'left open' the question of the Act's validity, allowing the appellant to argue the point in the future criminal trial.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the order of suspension was in violation of Rule 7 of the All-India Service (Appeal and Discipline) Rules, 1955, as the appellant contended it did not meet the criteria of sub-rule (1) and was not made under sub-rule (3).
appellant_arguments: The suspension order was made under sub-rule (1) of Rule 7, which requires an initiated disciplinary proceeding, but the order did not satisfy the provisions of this rule.
The suspension order was not made under sub-rule (3) of Rule 7, which allows for suspension pending a criminal investigation or trial.
respondent_arguments: The order of suspension must be read in the context of the entire case, which involves a pending investigation and trial relating to a criminal charge against the appellant, justifying the suspension under sub-rule (3) of Rule 7.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the suspension order was invalid because the report of the Central Bureau of Investigation was allegedly made mala fide.
appellant_arguments: The order of suspension was based on a report that was made mala fide, and therefore, the order itself was bad.
respondent_arguments: The appellant failed to prove mala fides as he did not name any specific person who acted in that manner.
To succeed, the appellant had to prove the order was made mala fide or for collateral purposes, and he neither alleged nor established either of these.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946, was ultra vires and the investigation was invalid.
appellant_arguments: The appellant raised the contention that the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946, was ultra vires and the investigation was invalid, but chose not to seek a decision on this point in the current appeal, intending to raise it in the pending criminal case.
respondent_arguments: The text indicates that the appellant did not want a decision on this point in this appeal and wished to raise it in the criminal case instead. The Court, therefore, left the contention open. As the issue was not pressed by the appellant, no arguments were made by the respondent on this point.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A government may place a member of the All-India Service under suspension at its discretion when an investigation, inquiry, or trial relating to a criminal charge is pending against that member. The validity of such a suspension order is assessed based on whether it was made in honest exercise of the powers conferred by the rule, not on the correctness of the underlying investigation report.
obiter: The validity of the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946, can be raised as a contention in a separate criminal trial.
Affidavits filed by parties that lack proper verification are deficient.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the suspension order was validly issued under sub-rule (3) of Rule 7, not sub-rule (1), as it must be read in the context of the pending criminal investigation and trial against the appellant. The court distinguished between the Central Bureau of Investigation's report and the government's subsequent suspension order, holding that any alleged mala fides in the report were not relevant to the validity of the order itself, which was found to be an honest exercise of power based on the government's satisfaction that suspension was necessary.
legal_tests_applied: Whether the order of suspension was warranted by the rule and also whether it was in honest exercise of powers.
An order of suspension has to be read in the context of the entire case to determine its legal basis.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's contention that the suspension order was made under sub-rule (1) of Rule 7 was rejected because the order itself made no reference to that sub-rule, and the facts of the case—a pending investigation and trial—clearly placed it under sub-rule (3).

The allegation of mala fides against the Central Bureau of Investigation was deemed irrelevant because the court's inquiry was limited to the validity of the suspension order, not the correctness or propriety of the underlying report.
The appellant failed to establish that the Government itself acted mala fide in issuing the suspension order, as there was no allegation against any particular government officer.
why_respondent_won: The court agreed that the order of suspension must be read in the context of the entire case, which involved an investigation and pending trial relating to a criminal charge, justifying the suspension under sub-rule (3) of Rule 7.
The court focused on the suspension order itself, which it found satisfied the rule and was an honest exercise of power, separate from the CBI report.

The court found that the text of the suspension order, which recited serious allegations, a prima facie case, and the government's satisfaction that suspension was necessary, demonstrated that the government had properly applied its mind.
policy_considerations: In view of the fact that the criminal case is pending, it is desirable not to express any opinion on the merits and demerits of the charges as also the rival contentions of the parties because such an opinion may cause prejudice.
